q: why did the Maya abandon their cities
why did the Maya civilization collapse
why did the Maya civilization abandon their great cities
what happened to the Maya civilization
a: The Maya civilization did not completely disappear, but the Classic Maya collapse between approximately 800 and 1000 CE saw the abandonment of many major cities in the southern lowlands of present-day Guatemala, Belize, and Mexico. The collapse was not caused by a single factor but by a combination of interconnected problems. The primary cause was likely severe, multi-century droughts that archaeological evidence from lake sediments and stalagmites confirms hit the region between 800 and 1000 CE. These droughts disrupted agriculture, which was already strained by overpopulation and deforestation. The Maya had cleared vast areas of forest for farming and building materials, which reduced rainfall and exacerbated drought conditions through a feedback loop. Deforestation also led to soil erosion, further reducing agricultural productivity. Political instability and increased warfare between city-states, possibly over dwindling resources, added to the stress. Trade networks collapsed as cities declined. The failure of Maya rulers to appease the gods during the drought (since Maya kings claimed to have divine connections to weather) may have led to revolts and the overthrow of ruling dynasties. However, the Maya did not entirely disappear — millions of Maya people still live in the region today, and cities in the northern Yucatan like Chichen Itza and Mayapan continued to thrive for several more centuries before their own declines.
